title: The Tomato Plant Affair
text:
Ravi had been certain that pruning a tomato plant was simple. “You just remove the extra leaves so the energy goes to the fruit,” he told Anuradha one Saturday morning, holding the small pair of garden scissors like a surgeon about to perform a delicate operation.
Anuradha, kneeling nearby and transplanting coriander, looked up, her eyebrow lifting in that way wives have perfected over centuries. “Hmm,” she said, a sound that contained neither agreement nor approval. She returned to her work, but a faint smile tugged at the corner of her lips.
When Ravi was done, the tomato plant looked… considerably lighter. “See? Perfect,” he said, stepping back with pride.
Anuradha stood, walked over, and silently began repositioning the branches. She tied one to a stake, loosened another, muttering softly under her breath, the sort of mumbling that husbands are never meant to hear word-for-word, but which generally translates to men and their confidence…
Ravi pretended not to notice, but the next morning, while she was inside making tea, he went back to the plant. He removed the stake she had tied, shifted a branch that he thought needed more sunlight, and even plucked a small leaf she had clearly left alone.
The following day, Anuradha “adjusted” it again. Ravi “corrected” it again the next morning. It became a silent relay race, neither mentioning it, both certain they were right, the tomato plant their unwitting referee.
After a week of this quiet sabotage, they noticed the plant looking a little weary. A few leaves had curled at the edges; one branch hung lower than usual. Ravi frowned. Anuradha crouched beside it and in a tone reserved for children who had scraped their knees, said, “Poor thing, caught between two stubborn people.”
They decided, without discussing it, to stop touching it for a while. Days passed. They watered it, talked near it, even praised its resilience, but kept their hands off. Slowly, the plant straightened, its leaves smoothing back into health.
One morning, Anuradha spotted the first small green tomato peeking shyly from behind a leaf. She called out, “Ravi! Come see.”
They stood together, looking at the little fruit as though it were a medal the plant had awarded itself for surviving their interference. Ravi chuckled. “So it turns out the plant knows better than both of us.” Anuradha smiled, eyes twinkling. “Next time, we’ll let it do the pruning.”
And that evening, while watering, Ravi gently tied a new branch to a stake, this time in exactly the way Anuradha would have done it.

title: Stories
text:
I grew up in the 90s in India, and like many of us, I found myself drawn into the gentle, ordinary-yet-magical worlds R.K. Narayan created. His stories taught me that the simplest words can hold entire universes, and that’s the spirit I carry into my own writing. What you’ll find here are glimpses from my own life: moments of trying to make sense of this journey, building a home, and leaning on the quiet strength of my family. In some ways, these stories are mine; in other ways, they’re echoes of a style and a spirit that shaped how I learned to see and tell them.

title: Second Chances
text:
When Ravi and Anuradha decided to start a garden, they had very different strategies.
Anuradha came home from the nursery one afternoon with a cardboard box full of mismatched, sickly saplings. Some had drooping leaves, others looked like they had given up hope entirely. She set the box down with the confidence of a doctor who had never lost a patient. “These,” she declared, “just need love, sunlight, and good soil.”
Ravi, meanwhile, had arrived from the same nursery with exactly two purchases: a pair of healthy-looking tomato plants. “Why spread yourself thin?” he said. “I’ll focus on quality over quantity.” He said it as if he had been running tomato farms for generations, though his gardening résumé consisted of once emptying the tulsi plant’s saucer for his mother.
Anuradha set about her project methodically: trimming dead bits, repotting, mixing compost, and talking to each plant in low, affectionate tones. Ravi, on the other hand, experimented, sometimes watering his tomatoes twice a day, sometimes forgetting entirely. He fed them fertilizer meant for roses because “nutrients are nutrients,” staked them too tightly so the stems bent, and once left them in the hottest patch of sun all afternoon because he thought “more sun equals more growth.”
Within a month, Anuradha’s sickly saplings had perked up, leaves shiny and upright. Ravi’s two tomato plants had given up their brief, bewildering life and dried into brittle stalks.
To his credit, Ravi didn’t sulk. “Fine,” he said one Saturday, “I’ve learned from my mistakes. This time, I’ll do it right.” He went back to the nursery and returned with two new tomato plants, placing them in the garden like honored guests. “You’ll see,” he told Anuradha, “this time I’ll get so many tomatoes, we’ll have to give some away.”
Anuradha smiled, said nothing, and quietly made her own plan.
When Ravi was at work, she would check his plants: loosening the ties if they were too tight, watering them just enough, pinching off a few leaves to help airflow. She worked invisibly, careful not to disturb the placement of his watering can or move the small stones he had set around the base “for luck.” In the evenings, Ravi would inspect his plants, beaming. “See? They’re thriving under my care.”
Weeks passed. The garden flourished. Anuradha’s revived saplings began to flower and bear fruit. Beans dangled from their vines, brinjals swelled, chillies gleamed bright green. And in the middle of it all stood Ravi’s tomato plants, full and lush, each branch heavy with ripening fruit.
One Saturday morning, they harvested their bounty together: brinjals in one basket, beans in another, and tomatoes in a bowl that overflowed onto the counter. Ravi picked up the largest one, held it in his palm like a trophy, and said, “I told you, I’m a natural at this.”
Anuradha, arranging the chillies in a plate, only smiled.
That evening, they cooked together, a meal fit for a king. Brinjal curry, beans stir-fry, and a tomato pachadi that was tangy and bright. Over dinner, Ravi declared, “Next season, I’m going to grow capsicum. Should be easy after this.”
Anuradha looked at him with fond amusement, thinking of the quiet mornings spent tending his plants. “Yes,” she said softly, “I’m sure you’ll do wonderfully.”
And in that moment, the garden seemed to hum in agreement with a quiet chorus from leaves, vines, and blossoms that knew the truth of how they had come to thrive.

title: Pumpkin
text:
Anuradha had grown up in a coastal town where people could still tell the time of day by the tilt of a coconut tree’s shadow and had lfowering shrubs in their balconies. She had an intuitive sense of when the breeze would turn warm, which flowers bees preferred, and which vegetables grew sulky if watered at the wrong hour.
Ravi, by contrast, had spent his childhood in a Chennai apartment where the only greenery was the tulsi plant his mother watered with such reverence that he never dared touch it. Gardening, to him, was something that happened in other people’s lives, like running a dairy farm or owning a pet elephant.
When they bought their modest home in Padmavathi Colony, it came with a narrow strip of backyard soil and a mango tree. Anuradha saw an invitation; Ravi saw extra sweeping work after the leaves fell.
On their very first weekend in the new house, Anuradha declared, “We’ll start a kitchen garden.” She said it with the tone of someone reading out a wedding date — fixed and beyond discussion. Ravi nodded, coffee in hand, making a mental note to keep an eye on the water bill.
The backyard soon filled with ambitious seedlings: brinjal, lady’s finger, beans, green chillies, and pumpkin, the last one chosen over Ravi’s mild objection. “They’ll take over everything,” he warned. “They’ll give shade,” she countered.
Their styles could not have been more different. Ravi measured distances between plants with a ruler, calculated watering schedules from the weather forecast, and proudly built a drip irrigation system from spare pipes. Anuradha relied entirely on touch and instinct. “They’re thirsty today,” she would say, feeling the leaves, without so much as glancing at a chart.
Arguments were gentle, almost rehearsed. “You’re overwatering.” “You’re under-loving.”
The vegetables grew in their own fashion. The brinjal plant yielded exactly three fruits: one perfectly round, one lopsided, and one looking as if it had been designed by accident. The pumpkin vine spread like a conqueror, curling around bean stakes, climbing the clothesline, and once, clinging stubbornly to Ravi’s forgotten flip-flop.
One evening, Ravi returned from work to find Anuradha holding a small yellow pumpkin flower, her face lit up as though she had found a long-lost friend. “Look,” she said softly.
He took it with mock solemnity. “I think you love these plants more than you love me.” “Don’t be silly,” she replied. “I can’t make sambar out of you.”
Over the months, the backyard became a shared language. Ravi grudgingly admitted that her guesswork often outperformed his careful calculations. Anuradha, in turn, trusted his irrigation system during the summer’s fiercest heat.
After dinner, they would sit in plastic chairs under the mango tree, watching the plants sway in the night breeze. The moonlight would lay silver across the pumpkin leaves, and Anuradha would lean lightly on his shoulder. No one spoke. There was nothing to improve upon in that moment.
Not every plant bore fruit, and not every season was kind. But tending together, through mistakes, small triumphs, and the occasional flip-flop entanglement, was its own reward.
That year, when they harvested their first pumpkin, Ravi carried it into the kitchen like a prize. Anuradha made pumpkin spiced appams, and they ate them hot, teasing each other over who had the bigger share.
Somewhere outside, the pumpkin vines listened, their leaves rustling faintly, as if amused by the two humans who thought they were in charge.
